summary.text: The Antarctic Circumpolar Current, also called the West Wind Drift, is an ocean current that flows from west to east all the way around Antarctica.
Driven by strong westerly winds, it carries an estimated 137 million cubic metres of water per second, making it the largest ocean current.
Because no landmass joins Antarctica, the current can circle the continent, keeping warm water away so Antarctica can keep its huge ice sheet.

paragraphs.heading: A ring around Antarctica
paragraphs.text: The Antarctic Circumpolar Current, or ACC, flows from west to east all the way around Antarctica. Seen from the South Pole, it turns clockwise. It is also called the West Wind Drift. It is the main feature of the Southern Ocean's circulation, moving an estimated 137 ± 7 sverdrups, that is 137 million cubic metres of water every second, and it is the largest ocean current.

paragraphs.heading: Why it matters
paragraphs.text: The current can circle the continent because no land links Antarctica to anywhere else. By flowing all the way round, it keeps warm ocean water away, which lets Antarctica hold on to its huge ice sheet. It also links the Atlantic, Pacific and Indian Oceans and is a main route for water to pass between them.

paragraphs.heading: Pushed by the westerlies
paragraphs.text: Strong westerly winds blowing across the Southern Ocean drive the current. Where there are continents, wind can simply heap light surface water against the coast, but the Southern Ocean has no such wall to push against. As the winds add eastward push, the Coriolis force nudges the water away from Earth's axis of spin, which here means northward. Deep down, below the main undersea ridges, a southward flow driven by pressure balances this. Swirling eddies and large bends in the current may also carry the wind's push down into the deep, and both effects are probably important.

paragraphs.heading: Size and speed
paragraphs.text: At the Drake Passage the current carries about 135 sverdrups, roughly 135 times the flow of all the world's rivers put together. A little more water joins in the Indian Ocean, and south of Tasmania the flow reaches around 147 sverdrups. Three fronts go with it, the Subantarctic Front, the Polar Front and the Southern ACC Front, and most of the water moves in the middle two. Over the Macquarie Ridge south of New Zealand it moves at about 4 km/h.

paragraphs.heading: A rich feeding ground
paragraphs.text: Along the current lies the Antarctic Convergence, where cold Antarctic water meets warmer subantarctic water. Nutrients well up there. They feed large amounts of phytoplankton, which support copepods and krill. Those in turn feed food chains that include fish, whales, seals, penguins and albatrosses.

paragraphs.heading: Sailors and the clipper route
paragraphs.text: Sailors have known this current for centuries. It speeds up any voyage from west to east but makes sailing the other way extremely hard, though the steady westerly winds are the main reason. Rounding Cape Horn westbound, on the clipper route from New York to California, was a notorious struggle. Going the other way, the fastest sailing route around the world rides the current past three capes: Cape Agulhas in Africa, South East Cape in Australia and Cape Horn in South America.

paragraphs.heading: How it began
paragraphs.text: Estimates of when the current started differ, but it is commonly placed at the boundary between the Eocene and Oligocene epochs. It formed as Antarctica became cut off, when the Tasmanian Passage and the Drake Passage opened after the land bridge to Antarctica broke apart. The Tasmanian Seaway is reported to have opened 33.5 million years ago. The date for the Drake Passage is more disputed, with estimates between 20 and 40 million years ago.
